extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, IP academics, policymakers, and others interested in patent examination and patent quality/policy
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how examiner characteristics, time allocation, and procedural rules affect patent grant rates and patent quality, and considering policy tradeoffs for changing examination resources or standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time allocated per application
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of hours the PTO allocates per application (which varies by examiner GS level and is 'roughly halved as the examiner rises in the ranks from GS-7 to GS-14') is a key determinant of grant behavior and patent quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frakes & Wasserman find that controlling for decreased time per application changes the inferred effect of experience on grants; the paper estimates that if all examiners had as much time as those with the most generous allocations, the PTO would grant nearly 20% fewer patents per year. Use hours-per-application as a primary explanatory variable when studying examination outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner experience vs grant rate
rubrics_metrics.description: More experienced examiners generally grant more patents (as shown by Lemley & Sampat), but after controlling for time per application, 'experienced examiners actually grant fewer patents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not interpret raw correlations between experience and grant rate without accounting for confounders like time allocation; include controls for time per application and GS-level in analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage behavior and time-intensive rejections (obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: When time per application decreases, 'examiners are particularly less likely to make time-intensive obviousness rejections,' implying triage toward quicker decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure specific types of rejections (e.g., §103/obviousness) as outcomes; interpret changes in rejection composition as evidence of time-driven triage rather than purely doctrinal shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent quality proxies (citations and renewal rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-grant indicators such as subsequent citations and renewal rates are used as proxies for patent quality, though their validity as indicators of which patents are 'good' is debated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple quality metrics but treat them cautiously; the author brackets whether proxies like subsequent citations and renewal rate 'in fact tell us which are the "good" patents.' Consider robustness checks using different quality measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust empirical testing (balanced panels and controls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical work should include careful tests such as balanced panels of examiners who experienced each promotion and controls for application-level factors (e.g., whether there is an RCE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Frakes & Wasserman's example of adding controls and using balanced panels to check that results are not driven by promotion timing or application mix; report multiple specification checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address selection/promotion-speed confounders
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners promoted more quickly up the GS scale may be different from those who linger; this selection could affect observed grant rates ('a caveat they can't address is that examiners who are promoted more quickly ... may be different').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for heterogeneity in promotion trajectories (e.g., quick risers vs lingerers) or acknowledge limitations; note the observed pattern that the grant rate for quick risers falls with experience after they reach GS-14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare administrative costs vs social benefits (welfare tradeoff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about increasing examiner time should be made by comparing the administrative cost of added scrutiny (higher PTO running costs) with benefits such as fewer litigation costs, reduced uncertainty for innovators, and lower consumer costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform cost-benefit/welfare analyses when recommending resource changes—e.g., calculate PTO salary increases needed to give more time and compare with estimates of litigation and social costs avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider nonzero optimality of 'bad' grants
rubrics_metrics.description: The optimal number of 'bad' patent grants is not necessarily zero (drawing on Kitch and Lemley's 'rational ignorance' argument); some erroneous grants may be socially tolerable given examination costs and uncertainty about a patent's future importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy recommendations should recognize that eliminating all invalid grants may be inefficient; weigh marginal costs of additional examination against marginal social benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate substitution of standards with brighter-line rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A full analysis should consider the benefits of replacing time-consuming substantive standards with brighter-line rules that may reduce examiner time per application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether rule-like standards could reduce examiner burden and improve decision consistency, and include this as an alternative policy lever in evaluations of examination reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational metric: patents granted per year
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of patents granted per year is a measurable outcome affected by examiner time allocations; Frakes & Wasserman estimate nearly a 20% reduction in grants if all examiners had entry-level time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregate grant counts as a policy-relevant outcome when estimating the effect of changes to examiner time or staffing; translate time changes into expected changes in grants to inform budgetary decisions.
